To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Th1 and Th2 subsets are characterized by distinct patterns of homing receptors and chemokine receptors, which are differentially expressed on the cells and which are involved in the regulation of their migration and function.
Th1 cells preferentially express selectins, CCR5 and CXCR3 whereas Th2 cells preferentially express CCR3, CCR4 and CCR8.

Th1 cells express the chemokine receptor CCR5 and the chemokines MIP-1alpha, RANTES and MCP-3 and that Th2 cells express CCR8 and the chemokine TARC, whereas CCR3, CCR4 and CXCR4 are expressed by both subsets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapeutic agents to treat inflammatory disorders.
the regulation of T cell differentiation, with the development of Th subsets, and with the mechanisms of their homing to sites of inflammation and tissue destruction.
the development of novel therapeutic agents that target specific immune responses, such as Th1/Th2 responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Th subsets do differ in their expression of adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors, and that this might be of importance for their trafficking into inflamed tissues.
Th1 cells are more efficient in entering inflammatory sites than Th2 cells.
the expression of chemokine receptors on T cells is not a simple matter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Th1 cells are the main effector cell in the development of inflammation.
Th1 and Th2 cells have different chemokine receptor repertoires and that this is a consequence of the differential regulation of chemokine receptors by the Th1 and Th 2 cytokines.
Th1 cells are more efficient in homing and migration to inflammatory sites than Th2 cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the functional specialization of T helper (Th) effector cells according not only to the cytokines that they secrete but also to the chemokine receptors that they express may provide a new level of understanding of the regulation of locally controlled immune responses.

the functional specialization of T helper cells according to cytokines secreted is not the sole determinant for the local immune response, but that T helper cells also differ in their homing and trafficking properties.
there is no single molecule, but rather a complex network of interactions that determine the migration of T cells to sites of inflammation.
